newsitem.title: GERMANY: BZW strategists cuts U.S. equity market rating.
newsitem.headline: BZW strategists cuts U.S. equity market rating.

text.p: As the bulls continue their rampage through the U.S. stock markets, BZW Bank has cut its recommendation for equity markets in the United States from overweight to neutral.

The rating change is based on the strength of recent performance and higher-than-expected fourth quarter corporate earnings in the U.S., but Michael Hughes, the bank's global head of economics and strategy, remains upbeat.

"I am very much an optimist and make no apologies for that. We don't believe that the long-term bull market, which dates back to 1981, is over -- certainly not until the Dow Jones starts with an eight," Hughes told a seminar on global investment perspectives.
There are still over 1,100 points to go before the Dow "starts with an eight", i.e., hits the 8,000-point threshold.
Hughes does not anticipate this level being breached in 1997 and foresees a period in which the Dow will "tread water". Hughes also forecast a cut in U.S. interest rates within a year.

Moving back across the Atlantic, Hughes has similarly cut his rating on European stock markets to neutral. One of the main issues facing Europe was currency union and the attendant problem of stimulating growth.
Hughes does not think that EMU will act as a panacea for Europe's ills, however.

Optimism on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) was overextended and the degree of fiscal restraint practised by many would-be member states was unprecedented. Consequently, economic growth post-EMU could prove disappointing.
"Europe needs a growth stimulus. The euro, when it does emerge, might be weaker than people think, in order to stimulate demand," said Hughes.

In the run-up to currency union, further currency weakness could be expected to kick-start demand and Hughes forecast a weakening of the deutschemark-dollar rate by anything between 10 or 15 percent, to near 1.80 marks to the dollar.
"We are working on the basis that currency union will take place and that it will last longer than people think. This year markets will have to digest the idea of currency union," said Hughes.
"The downsides of EMU are the effect on demand because of Maastricht-related fiscal restraint," said Hughes.
Hughes' money is on Asia, especially China, which has fallen in and out of favour among emerging market analysts in recent years, but seems to be back in the international investor's good books.
Good news for China will help Japan, where the economic growth has been at best sluggish in recent years.

"The Chinese austerity programme seems to be over and we are looking to upgrade Japan because of China -- China is a big consumer of electronics and could be one of the few growth stimuli for Japan," said Hughes.
"We view Japan as a trading environment rather than a growth environment and we are looking at very modest long-term growth rates in Japan of two percent, or two-and-a-half percent.
